passage:
Thursday, late.

They announced it at 11 today: I'm the new senior associate. My phone lit up all afternoon, and I was happy for about an hour.

Then Nazia walked past my desk without looking up. We've had lunch together nearly every day for two years. She left the office at five sharp with her headphones on, and I felt like I'd done something wrong.

I keep wanting to say sorry. But I worked hard for this, and Nazia knows it. So I didn't apologise and I didn't post anything. I just left a sticky note on her monitor: "Your template saved my first client deck. Thank you. Lunch whenever." 🙂

Maybe the silence is disappointment about her own year, not about me. I'll give it time.

Shreya

qa.q: What did Shreya leave on Nazia's monitor?
qa.a: Shreya left a sticky note thanking Nazia for the template that saved a first client deck and offering lunch whenever Nazia was ready.

qa.q: What does Shreya think might explain Nazia's silence?
qa.a: Shreya thinks the silence may be Nazia's disappointment about Nazia's own year rather than dislike of Shreya, so it is not treated as proof of anger.

qa.q: What did Shreya do well in handling the cold shoulder?
qa.a: Shreya neither apologised for earning the role nor flaunted it; the note credited Nazia's help and left space for the friendship to recover.

qa.q: How might Nazia be feeling as she walks past the desk?
qa.a: Nazia may be feeling the sting of comparison and needing space, so the promotion could feel like a loss for her even though she is fond of Shreya.

grounding: Shreya, newly promoted, senses a friend turning cold and responds by staying warm, crediting the help and allowing time.

passage:
The day Keerthana's promotion to shift lead was pinned on the notice board of the Chennai call centre, Tenzin stopped saving her a seat in the canteen. They had trained together, covered each other's breaks, shared auto fares home for two years.
Keerthana felt the chill like a draught. She didn't post about the promotion. She also didn't say sorry for it.
At the Friday team meeting she said, "Half of what I know about calming angry callers, I learned from Tenzin's desk." Tenzin looked up, surprised, then looked away.
Keerthana kept things simple after that: a "good morning", a samosa left on Tenzin's desk on a long day, no pressure to talk. She guessed the distance might be about losing their old evenings together, not about hating her.
In the third week, Tenzin sat down across from her at lunch. "Pass the pickle."

qa.q: How long had Keerthana and Tenzin shared auto fares home?
What was Keerthana feeling when Tenzin stopped saving her a seat?
qa.a: She felt a chill of hurt and sadness at the distance, like a draught, yet she did not feel she had to apologise.

qa.q: How did Keerthana handle the friendship after her promotion?
qa.a: She credited Tenzin publicly, didn't flaunt the promotion, stayed warm in small ways, and gave the friendship time without pressure.

qa.q: How might Tenzin be feeling after the promotion?
qa.a: Tenzin may feel envious and also sad about losing their old evenings together, which is why the coldness slowly eases.

grounding: A friend turns cold after the protagonist's promotion; she neither apologises nor flaunts it, credits the friend's help, and gives the friendship time.

passage:
"Lokesh, you've been eating at your desk all week."
"Busy."
"Since my promotion was announced?"
Lokesh kept typing. "Congratulations, Harish. Really. You deserved it."
"You helped me get it. That client migration last year, you stayed back with me three nights. I said that to the director, you know."
Lokesh's hands paused. "You did?"
"I did. And I'm not going to pretend I don't want the job. I do. But I miss our lunches."
"It's weird, man. We applied for the same thing."
"I know. Take your time. I'm not going anywhere."
"You're my boss now, technically."
"Technically. But I'm still the one who can't order at the dosa place without you."
Lokesh almost smiled. "Friday. Not before."
"Friday."

qa.q: How many nights did Lokesh stay back with Harish during the client migration?
What might Lokesh be feeling when he says "It's weird, man"?
qa.a: He probably feels envious and sad, having applied for the same job, and awkward now that Harish is his boss.

qa.q: What did Harish do that helped the friendship?
qa.a: He credited Lokesh's help to the director, did not apologise for wanting the job, said he missed their lunches, and gave Lokesh time.

qa.q: If you were Harish, what would you want from Lokesh?
qa.a: Harish wants the friendship back and understands that Lokesh needs space for a loss, so he patiently accepts "Friday. Not before."

grounding: A friend turns cold after the protagonist's promotion; he credits the friend's help, stays warm without apologising, and gives the friendship time.
